title: Health and the body
objectives: I can name the parts of the body and say what hurts with 'У ме́не боли́ть...' and 'У ме́не боля́ть...', making the verb agree with the body part.
I can use the plural of 'о́ко', which is 'о́чі', 'оче́й' and 'очи́ма', and the regular plural of 'ву́хо', which is 'ву́ха' and 'вух'.
I can say what someone must, should or needs to do with 'му́сити', 'пови́нен', 'тре́ба' and 'ва́рто', and give advice with the imperative.
I can ask how someone feels and what is wrong, and describe my symptoms to a doctor and a pharmacist.
I can explain why 'о́ко' has 'ч' in 'о́чі', why 'ка́шель' loses its 'е' in 'ка́шлю', and how 'се́рце' and 'пови́нна' are said.

vocabulary.note: The plural is irregular: 'о́чі', genitive 'оче́й', instrumental 'очи́ма'. The second grammar note explains it.

example.source: Oksana has blue eyes.

vocabulary.note: The plural is regular: 'ву́ха', genitive plural 'вух'.

example.source: The child has an earache.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'зу́ба', plural 'зу́би', genitive plural 'зубі́в'.

example.target: Тара́с ду́же лю́бить цу́кор, і за́раз у ньо́го боли́ть зуб.
example.source: Taras loves sugar, and now he has a toothache.
example.source_literal: Taras very loves sugar, and now at him hurts tooth.

vocabulary.note: 'У ме́не боли́ть го́рло.' means 'I have a sore throat'.

example.target: Коли́ в ме́не боли́ть го́рло, я п’ю бага́то ча́ю.
example.source: When I have a sore throat, I drink a lot of tea.
example.source_literal: When at me hurts throat, I drink much of-tea.

vocabulary.note: 'У ме́не боли́ть спи́на.' means 'my back hurts'.

example.target: Мико́ла бага́то працю́є, тому́ в ньо́го ча́сто боли́ть спи́на.
example.source: Mykola works a lot, so his back often hurts.
example.source_literal: Mykola much works, therefore at him often hurts back.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'живота́'. 'У ме́не боли́ть живі́т.' means 'I have a stomachache'.

example.target: Ді́ти ї́ли бага́то полуни́ць, і в них боли́ть живі́т.
example.source: The children ate a lot of strawberries, and they have stomachaches.
example.source_literal: Children ate many of-strawberries, and at them hurts belly.

vocabulary.note: Plural 'серця́', with the stress on the ending. As in English, the word also names a person's feelings: 'до́бре се́рце' is a kind heart.

example.source: My grandmother has a bad heart.

vocabulary.note: Second conjugation. The body part that hurts is the subject, so in the present only 'боли́ть' and 'боля́ть' are used; past 'болі́в', 'болі́ла', 'болі́ло', 'болі́ли'. Its perfective partner 'заболі́ти' means to begin to hurt.

example.source: Yesterday I had a headache.

vocabulary.note: First conjugation, like 'розумі́ти': 'хворі́ю', 'хворі́єш'. Its perfective partner 'захворі́ти' means to fall ill.

example.source: My brother has been ill for a week.

vocabulary.note: 'Я хво́рий.' for a man, 'Я хво́ра.' for a woman. Said of a body part, it means weak or diseased: 'хво́ре се́рце'.

example.source: Oksana is ill today; she is at home.

vocabulary.note: The noun for health is 'здоро́в’я'. 'Будь здоро́вий!' and 'Бу́дьте здоро́ві!' are wishes; the culture note explains them.

example.source: My grandfather is old but healthy.

vocabulary.note: 'почува́юся', 'почува́єшся', 'почува́ється'. It names how a person feels in body or mood and takes an adverb: 'до́бре', 'пога́но'. Its perfective partner, 'почу́тися', is rare.

example.source: I feel unwell today.

vocabulary.note: 'У ме́не температу́ра.' means 'I have a fever'. Body temperature in Ukraine is measured in degrees Celsius, and a fever begins at about thirty-seven and a half degrees.

example.source: The child has a temperature of thirty-nine.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'лі́ків'. Whether it names one medicine or several, the word is plural, and so are its adjectives and verbs: 'ці лі́ки', 'лі́ки ко́штують'. Medicine for an illness takes 'від' and the genitive: 'лі́ки від ка́шлю'.

example.target: Ці лі́ки тре́ба пи́ти пі́сля ї́жі.
example.source: This medicine should be taken after meals.
example.source_literal: These medicine necessary to-drink after food.

vocabulary.note: Locative 'у лі́карні'. The word shares its root with 'лі́кар' and 'лі́ки'; the suffix '-ня' names a place.

example.source: Olena works at the hospital.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ка́шлю': the 'е' drops out when an ending is added.

example.target: Ді́ти не спа́ли вночі́, бо в них був ка́шель.
example.source: The children didn't sleep at night because they were coughing.
example.source_literal: Children not slept at-night, because at them was cough.

vocabulary.note: 'У ме́не засту́да.' means 'I have a cold'. The word names the illness only; a cold day is described with 'хо́лодно'.

example.target: У Се́ма засту́да, тому́ він сиди́ть удо́ма.
example.source: Sam has a cold, so he is staying at home.
example.source_literal: At Sam cold, therefore he sits at-home.

vocabulary.note: Second conjugation: 'му́шу', 'му́сиш', 'му́сять'. The 'с' becomes 'ш' only in the 'я' form. It has no perfective partner. An infinitive follows.

example.source: I have to work tomorrow.

vocabulary.note: 'пови́нна', 'пови́нно', 'пови́нні'. It is used only as the predicate, agrees with the subject and takes an infinitive. It is not a verb; the third grammar note explains it.

example.target: Ти пови́нен пи́ти ці лі́ки три дні.
example.source: You should take this medicine for three days.
example.source_literal: You obliged to-drink these medicine three days.

vocabulary.note: The person is in the dative, and an infinitive follows. It gives friendly advice; 'не ва́рто' advises against something.

example.source: You should read this book.

dialogues.title: Olena visits Sam
dialogues.context: Sam has been ill for two days. Olena, Taras's sister, is a doctor, and she comes to Sam's apartment to see him. They are friends and say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Приві́т, Се́ме! Що з тобо́ю?
lines.source: Hi, Sam! What's wrong with you?
lines.source_literal: Hi, Sam! What with you?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Приві́т, Оле́но. Я вже два дні хво́рий.
lines.source: Hi, Olena. I've been ill for two days.
lines.source_literal: Hi, Olena. I already two days sick.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Як ти почува́єшся? Що в те́бе боли́ть?
lines.source: How are you feeling? What hurts?
lines.source_literal: How you feel? What at you hurts?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Боли́ть голова́ й ду́же боли́ть го́рло. А коли́ я чита́ю, боля́ть о́чі.
lines.source: I have a headache, and my throat is very sore. And when I read, my eyes hurt.
lines.source_literal: Hurts head and very hurts throat. And when I read, hurt eyes.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Температу́ра є?
lines.source: Do you have a fever?
lines.source_literal: Temperature is?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, три́дцять ві́сім. І вночі́ був ка́шель.
lines.source: Yes, thirty-eight. And I was coughing in the night.
lines.source_literal: Yes, thirty eight. And at-night was cough.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Це засту́да. Тобі́ тре́ба відпочива́ти. Ти му́сиш три дні сиді́ти вдо́ма.
lines.source: It's a cold. You need to rest. You have to stay at home for three days.
lines.source_literal: This cold. To-you necessary to-rest. You must three days to-sit at-home.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Три дні? Але́ за́втра я хо́чу бу́ти в університе́ті.
lines.source: Three days? But tomorrow I want to be at the university.
lines.source_literal: Three days? But tomorrow I want to-be in university.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ні, не ва́рто. Пий бага́то ча́ю й ма́ло говори́.
lines.source: No, you shouldn't. Drink lots of tea and don't talk much.
lines.source_literal: No, not worth. Drink much of-tea and little speak.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре. Мені́ тре́ба йти в лі́карню?
lines.source: All right. Do I need to go to the hospital?
lines.source_literal: Well. To-me necessary to-go to hospital?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ні, не тре́ба. Але́ купи́ в апте́ці лі́ки від ка́шлю.
lines.source: No, you don't. But buy some cough medicine at the pharmacy.
lines.source_literal: No, not necessary. But buy in pharmacy medicine from cough.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Апте́ка по́руч, я їх куплю́ сього́дні.
lines.source: The pharmacy is next door. I'll get it today.
lines.source_literal: Pharmacy nearby, I them will-buy today.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: До́бре. Оду́жуй, Се́ме!
lines.source: Good. Get well soon, Sam!
lines.source_literal: Good. Recover, Sam!

dialogues.title: At the pharmacy
dialogues.context: The pharmacy is next door to Sam's building, so he goes down to buy the medicine. Bohdan, the pharmacist, serves him. They do not know each other, so they say 'ви'.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий день. Що вас турбу́є?
lines.source: Good afternoon. What's bothering you?
lines.source_literal: Good day. What you bothers?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день. У ме́не ка́шель і боли́ть го́рло.
lines.source: Good afternoon. I have a cough and a sore throat.
lines.source_literal: Good day. At me cough and hurts throat.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: А температу́ра у вас є?
lines.source: And do you have a fever?
lines.source_literal: And temperature at you is?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Учо́ра була́, а сього́дні вже нема́є.
lines.source: I had one yesterday, but today it's gone.
lines.source_literal: Yesterday was, and today already there-is-not.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́бре. Ось лі́ки від ка́шлю. Пи́йте одну́ ло́жку пі́сля ї́жі.
lines.source: Good. Here is some cough medicine. Take one spoonful after meals.
lines.source_literal: Good. Here medicine from cough. Drink one spoon after food.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А для го́рла у вас щось є?
lines.source: And do you have anything for the throat?
lines.source_literal: And for throat at you something is?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Є. Ось, будь ла́ска. І вам ва́рто бага́то пи́ти.
lines.source: Yes, here you are. And you should drink plenty.
lines.source_literal: There-is. Here, be kindness. And to-you worth much to-drink.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Лі́карка сказа́ла: «Три дні вдо́ма». Але́ в понеді́лок я пови́нен співа́ти на конце́рті.
lines.source: The doctor said, 'Three days at home.' But on Monday I'm supposed to sing at a concert.
lines.source_literal: Doctor said: 'Three days at-home.' But on Monday I obliged to-sing at concert.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Якщо́ бу́дете відпочива́ти, до понеді́лка бу́дете здоро́ві.
lines.source: If you rest, you'll be well by Monday.
lines.source_literal: If will-be to-rest, till Monday will-be healthy.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую. Скі́льки ко́штують ці лі́ки?
lines.source: Thank you. How much is this medicine?
lines.source_literal: I-thank. How-much cost these medicine?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Сто два́дцять гри́вень.
lines.source: A hundred and twenty hryvnias.
lines.source_literal: Hundred twenty of-hryvnias.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ось, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: Here you are.
lines.source_literal: Here, be kindness.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Дя́кую. Бу́дьте здоро́ві!
lines.source: Thank you. Take care!
lines.source_literal: I-thank. Be healthy!

dialogues.title: A call to the teacher
dialogues.context: Sam cannot speak, so Oksana phones his teacher, Iryna Petrivna, for him. Iryna Petrivna answers with 'Слу́хаю', literally 'I-listen'. Oksana says 'ви' to her and addresses her by her first name and patronymic.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Слу́хаю.
lines.source: Hello?
lines.source_literal: I-listen.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́брий день, Іри́но Петрі́вно. Це Окса́на, по́друга Се́ма.
lines.source: Good afternoon, Iryna Petrivna. It's Oksana, Sam's friend.
lines.source_literal: Good day, Iryna Petrivna. This Oksana, friend of-Sam.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: До́брий день, Окса́но. Щось із Се́мом?
lines.source: Good afternoon, Oksana. Is something wrong with Sam?
lines.source_literal: Good day, Oksana. Something with Sam?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так. Він хво́рий, у ньо́го засту́да. Він не мо́же говори́ти, бо ду́же боли́ть го́рло.
lines.source: Yes. He's ill; he has a cold. He can't speak because his throat is very sore.
lines.source_literal: Yes. He sick, at him cold. He not can to-speak, because very hurts throat.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Як він почува́ється?
lines.source: How is he feeling?
lines.source_literal: How he feels?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Пога́но. У ньо́го температу́ра. Він му́сить три дні сиді́ти вдо́ма.
lines.source: Not well. He has a fever. He has to stay at home for three days.
lines.source_literal: Badly. At him temperature. He must three days to-sit at-home.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Звича́йно. Він пови́нен відпочива́ти. Хай нічо́го не чита́є й бага́то спить.
lines.source: Of course. He should rest. He shouldn't read anything, and he should sleep a lot.
lines.source_literal: Of-course. He obliged to-rest. Let nothing not reads and much sleeps.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́бре, я йому́ скажу́.
lines.source: All right, I'll tell him.
lines.source_literal: Good, I to-him will-tell.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А ви, Окса́но? Ви здоро́ві?
lines.source: And you, Oksana? Are you well?
lines.source_literal: And you, Oksana? You healthy?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, дя́кую, я почува́юся до́бре.
lines.source: Yes, thank you, I feel fine.
lines.source_literal: Yes, I-thank, I feel well.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: До́бре. Скажі́ть Се́мові, хай оду́жує.
lines.source: Good. Tell Sam to get well soon.
lines.source_literal: Good. Tell to-Sam, let recovers.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Скажу́. До поба́чення, Іри́но Петрі́вно!
lines.source: I will. Goodbye, Iryna Petrivna!
lines.source_literal: I-will-tell. Until seeing, Iryna Petrivna!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: До поба́чення, Окса́но.
lines.source: Goodbye, Oksana.
lines.source_literal: Until seeing, Oksana.

grammar.title: Saying what hurts: 'У ме́не боли́ть голова́'
grammar.explanation:
English usually makes the person the subject of a sentence about pain: 'I have a headache', 'my back hurts'. Ukrainian makes the aching body part the subject of the verb 'болі́ти', to hurt, and names the person the way it names an owner, with 'у' and the genitive, as in 'У ме́не є брат.' from the unit on family:

- 'У ме́не боли́ть голова́.' I have a headache, literally 'at me hurts head'.
- 'У Тара́са боли́ть живі́т.' Taras has a stomachache, literally 'at Taras hurts belly'.

Because the body part is the subject, the verb agrees with the body part, not with the person. In the present, 'болі́ти' in this meaning is used only in the forms for 'він' and 'вони́': 'боли́ть' for one thing, 'боля́ть' for several. In the past it takes the gender and number of the body part, and in the future it takes 'бу́де' or 'бу́дуть':

- 'боли́ть': 'У ме́не боли́ть зуб.'
- 'боля́ть': 'У ме́не боля́ть зу́би.'
- 'болі́в', 'болі́ла', 'болі́ло', 'болі́ли': 'Учо́ра в Окса́ни болі́ло го́рло.'
- 'бу́де болі́ти', 'бу́дуть болі́ти': 'За́втра в ньо́го бу́дуть болі́ти но́ги.'

'У ме́не' already says whose head it is, so Ukrainian adds no possessive such as 'моя́'. The verb usually comes before the body part, because the body part is the new information, and new information comes last. To ask what hurts, say 'Що в те́бе боли́ть?', or 'Що у вас боли́ть?' to someone you call 'ви'. The pronoun forms after 'у' are those of the unit on family: 'у ме́не', 'у тебе́', 'у ньо́го', 'у не́ї', 'у нас', 'у вас', 'у них', with 'в' instead of 'у' after a vowel by euphony, except before 'в': 'у вас' stays 'у' everywhere.

An illness or a symptom is named with the same 'у' and the genitive, and the illness itself is in the nominative: 'У ме́не засту́да.' (I have a cold), 'У ньо́го температу́ра.' (He has a fever), 'У не́ї ка́шель.' (She has a cough). The word 'є' is left out, because these sentences describe a state rather than say that something exists. With 'є', 'Температу́ра є?' asks whether there is any fever at all.

Three questions about health are learned whole:

- 'Як ти почува́єшся?' and 'Як ви почува́єтеся?' ask how someone is feeling. The answer uses an adverb: 'Я почува́юся до́бре.', 'Я почува́юся пога́но.'
- 'Що з тобо́ю?' or 'Що з ва́ми?', literally 'what with you?', asks what is wrong when someone looks unwell. 'Тобо́ю' and 'ва́ми' are the instrumental forms that follow 'з'.
- 'Що вас турбу́є?', literally 'what you bothers?', is the question a doctor or a pharmacist asks. 'Турбу́є' is the 'він' form of 'турбува́ти', to bother, and 'вас' is its object.

A state that began earlier and still continues takes the present tense in Ukrainian, with 'вже' and the length of time in the accusative: 'Я хворі́ю вже два дні.' (I have been ill for two days, literally 'I am-ill already two days'). English uses 'have been' for this.

The preposition 'від' takes the genitive and means 'from'. With a word for medicine it names the illness the medicine works against: 'лі́ки від ка́шлю' (cough medicine, literally 'medicine from cough'), 'лі́ки від температу́ри' (medicine for a fever).

rows: I had a sore throat yesterday.

examples.source: Taras's teeth hurt.
Oksana had a sore throat yesterday.
What hurts?
He has a cold and a fever.
What's wrong with you?

examples.target: Мені́ тре́ба купи́ти лі́ки від температу́ри.
examples.source: I need to buy some medicine for a fever.
examples.source_literal: To-me necessary to-buy medicine from temperature.

grammar.title: Body parts in the plural: 'о́чі' and 'ву́ха'
grammar.explanation:
Most words for parts of the body form their plural by the rules of the unit on the plural in every case. 'Рука́' and 'нога́' give 'ру́ки' and 'но́ги', with the stress moving to the stem as the unit on stress showed, and their genitive plurals are 'рук' and 'ніг'. 'Зуб' gives 'зу́би', genitive plural 'зубі́в'. Neuter nouns in '-о' take '-а' in the nominative plural and no ending in the genitive plural, and 'ву́хо', ear, follows them exactly:

- 'ву́хо', one ear
- 'ву́ха', ears
- 'вух', of ears, the genitive plural

Its other plural forms take the regular endings: 'ву́хам' in the dative and 'у ву́хах' in the locative.

'О́ко', eye, is different. Ukrainian once had a third number beside the singular and the plural, called the dual, for things that come in twos. The dual has disappeared, but the plural of 'о́ко' comes from it, and its stem changes from 'ок-' to 'оч-':

- 'о́чі', eyes, in the nominative and the accusative
- 'оче́й', of eyes, the genitive, with the stress on the ending
- 'оча́м' in the dative and 'в оча́х' in the locative
- 'очи́ма', with eyes, the instrumental, an old ending that only a few words keep

The singular is regular: 'о́ко', 'о́ка', 'о́ку', 'о́ком', 'в о́ці'. In 'в о́ці' the 'к' becomes 'ц' before the locative '-і', as in 'у руці́'.

After 'два', 'три' and 'чоти́ри' the noun is 'о́ка', not the plural 'о́чі': 'два о́ка й два ву́ха', two eyes and two ears.

The plural 'о́чі' takes plural adjectives and verbs, as every plural does: 'си́ні о́чі' (blue eyes) and 'боля́ть о́чі' (the eyes hurt). A description of a person uses 'у' and the genitive, as possession does: 'У Со́фії зеле́ні о́чі.' (Sofiia has green eyes, literally 'at Sofiia green eyes').

examples.source: Sofiia has green eyes.
I saw it with my own eyes.

examples.target: У ко́жної люди́ни два о́ка й два ву́ха.
examples.source: Every person has two eyes and two ears.
examples.source_literal: At each person two eyes and two ears.

grammar.title: Must, should and advice: 'му́сити', 'пови́нен', 'тре́ба', 'ва́рто'
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian has four common ways to say that someone must, should or needs to do something, and the imperative gives advice directly. They differ in strength and in structure, and the structure decides the case of the person.

'Му́сити' is a verb meaning 'must' or 'to have to'. It names a strong necessity, often one that circumstances impose. The person is its subject, in the nominative, and an infinitive follows. It is a verb of the second conjugation, and its 'с' becomes 'ш' only in the 'я' form:

- 'я му́шу', 'ти му́сиш', 'він му́сить'
- 'ми му́симо', 'ви му́сите', 'вони́ му́сять'
- past: 'му́сив', 'му́сила', 'му́сили'

'Пови́нен' means 'obliged' or 'should' and names a duty or what is right. It is not a verb but the short form of an adjective: a form without the full adjective ending, used only as the predicate. Like any adjective it agrees with the subject in gender and number, and an infinitive follows:

- 'він пови́нен'
- 'вона́ пови́нна'
- 'воно́ пови́нно'
- 'ми, ви, вони́ пови́нні'

In the past and the future, 'бу́ти' carries the tense, as in 'він був пови́нен' and 'вона́ бу́де пови́нна'. With 'ви', even to one person, the plural 'пови́нні' is used, as every adjective in the predicate is plural with 'ви': Sam says 'Ви пови́нні відпочива́ти.' (You should rest.) to his teacher, and Iryna Petrivna asks Oksana 'Ви здоро́ві?' (Are you well?).

'Тре́ба', which the unit on the dative taught, and 'ва́рто' are predicative words: each is the whole predicate of a sentence without a grammatical subject, and the person, when named, is in the dative. 'Тре́ба' says that something is necessary. 'Ва́рто', literally 'worth', says that something is worth doing, and it is the usual word for friendly advice: 'Тобі́ ва́рто пи́ти бага́то води́.' (You should drink lots of water.) Without a person they state a general rule: 'Тре́ба ми́ти ру́ки.' (One must wash one's hands.)

The imperative gives advice directly. The imperfective is used for advice about what to do in general or for some time: 'Відпочива́йте.', 'Пи́йте чай.', 'Не працю́йте сього́дні.'

Each of the four ways has its own job, and 'му́сити' is the strongest of them:

- 'му́сити': a necessity
- 'тре́ба': a need
- 'пови́нен': a duty
- 'ва́рто': advice

Negation needs care. English 'you must not' forbids, but 'Ти не му́сиш іти́.' only removes the obligation: it means 'You don't have to go'. To forbid, Ukrainian uses 'не мо́жна' with the dative: 'Тобі́ не мо́жна ї́сти цу́кор.' (You mustn't eat sugar, literally 'to-you not possible to-eat sugar'). 'Не ва́рто' advises against: 'Не ва́рто працюва́ти, коли́ ти хво́рий.' (You shouldn't work when you're ill.)

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: о́чі, се́рце, ка́шлю and пови́нна
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. These are the points the words for health and the body bring up.

'О́ко' has a hard 'к', but its plural 'о́чі' [ˈɔt͡ʃi] has 'ч'. This is an alternation, a regular change of one consonant into another within a word: 'к' becomes 'ч' in every plural form, all of which come from the old dual ('о́чі', 'оче́й', 'очи́ма'), just as 'к' becomes 'ц' before the locative '-і' ('в о́ці', 'у руці́'). The 'ч' is hard and only slightly softened before 'і'. In 'оче́й' [ɔˈt͡ʃɛj] the stress moves to the ending.

In 'се́рце' [ˈsɛrt͡sɛ] two consonants meet with no vowel between them, and both are said. The 'р' is hard, because 'р' is soft only before a vowel letter that softens it, and it is a single tap of the tongue; the 'ц' is hard before 'е'. In the plural 'серця́' [sɛrˈt͡sʲɑ] the 'ц' is soft before 'я', and the stress moves to the ending.

'Ка́шель' [ˈkɑʃɛlʲ] ends in a soft 'ль'. Its 'е' stands before the last consonant only while the word ends there; when an ending is added, the 'е' drops out, as in 'сі́чень', 'сі́чня'. So the genitive is 'ка́шлю' [ˈkɑʃlʲu], where 'ю' keeps the 'л' soft. The genitive ends in '-ю' because a cough is a state, not a countable thing, like the abstractions of the unit on family. 'Пови́нен' loses its 'е' in the same way, and in 'пови́нна' [pɔˈʋɪnːɑ], 'пови́нно' and 'пови́нні' [pɔˈʋɪnʲːi] the doubled 'нн' is one long consonant, soft before 'і'.

'Живі́т' has 'і' in its closed last syllable, and 'о' returns when an ending opens the syllable: 'живота́' [ʒɪʋɔˈtɑ], as 'кіт' gives 'кота́'. 'Нога́' shows the same rule the other way round: its genitive plural 'ніг' has no ending, so the syllable closes and 'о' becomes 'і'.

In 'му́шу' [ˈmuʃu] the 'с' of 'му́сити' becomes 'ш' in the 'я' form only, as 'д' becomes 'дж' in 'сиджу́' from 'сиді́ти'.

In 'болі́ти' the 'л' changes with the vowel after it. It is soft before 'і' and 'я' ('болі́ти', 'боля́ть' [bɔˈlʲɑtʲ]) and hard before 'и' ('боли́ть' [bɔˈlɪtʲ]).

The other new words follow the familiar rules:

- 'Зуб' ends in a voiced [b], as every voiced consonant at the end of a word does: [zub]. In the genitive plural 'зубі́в' the stress moves to the ending.
- In 'здоро́в’я' the apostrophe after 'в' keeps the 'в' hard and the [j] of 'я' sounded, as in 'м’я́со'.
- 'Лі́карня' [ˈlʲikɑrnʲɑ] has a hard 'р' before 'н' and a soft 'н' before 'я'.
- In 'почува́ється' the ending '-ться' is said [t͡sʲːɑ], as in 'прокида́ється'.
- In 'хво́рий', 'здоро́вий' and 'ву́хо' the 'в' stands before a vowel and is [ʋ].

culture.title: Wishing health, and the pharmacy
culture.text:
Health comes up in many everyday phrases. When someone sneezes, people say 'Будь здоро́вий!' to a man, 'Будь здоро́ва!' to a woman and 'Бу́дьте здоро́ві!' to someone they call 'ви', which literally means 'be healthy!'. The same words also serve as a warm goodbye or a thank-you. To someone who is ill, people say 'Оду́жуй!' or 'Оду́жуйте!', get well, from the verb 'оду́жувати', to recover. The noun 'здоро́в’я', health, is the first thing wished on a birthday, and a common toast is 'За здоро́в’я!', to health. Another toast is 'Бу́дьмо!', literally 'let us be', a first person plural imperative of 'бу́ти', to which the company answers 'Гей!'

Pharmacies are on almost every street of a Ukrainian city, and some stay open day and night. For a cold or a cough many people go first to the pharmacy, where the pharmacist asks about the symptoms and suggests a medicine. For anything more serious, people see their family doctor, 'сіме́йний лі́кар' or 'сіме́йна лі́карка', a doctor each person chooses and registers with. In an emergency the number for an ambulance is 103, and the general emergency number is 112.

Many families also trust home remedies for a cold:

- tea with honey, 'чай із ме́дом'
- tea with raspberry jam, 'чай із мали́новим варе́нням'
- garlic and onion, 'часни́к' and 'цибу́ля', eaten raw
- warm socks and plenty of rest

Many people also believe that a draft or cold feet can bring on a cold, so grandmothers remind children to wear a hat and keep their feet warm.

exercises.prompt: Match the parts of the body with their English names

choices: Taras is at the hospital today.

exercises.explanation: The three words share one root. 'Лі́ки' is medicine, 'лі́карка' is a woman doctor, and 'лі́карня', with the suffix '-ня' that names a place, is the hospital.
It is literally 'what you bothers?', the question a doctor or a pharmacist asks. The question 'Де боли́ть?' asks where it hurts.
The head is the subject, and 'голова́' is singular, so the verb is 'боли́ть'.
'О́чі' is plural and is the subject, so the verb is 'боля́ть'. The person, 'Тара́са', is in the genitive after 'у'.
'Зу́би' is plural and 'боля́ть' is the present plural. 'У ме́не боли́ть зуб.' is about one tooth, and 'болі́ли' is the past.
'О́ко' has the irregular plural 'о́чі', which comes from the old dual. 'О́ка' is the genitive singular and the form after 'два', and 'ву́ха' is the plural of 'ву́хо'.
After a preposition the genitive of 'вона́' is 'не́ї', with 'н' added: 'у не́ї'.
In the past the verb agrees with the body part. 'Живі́т' is masculine, so the form is 'болі́в'.

exercises.prompt: Why is the verb 'боля́ть' in 'У ме́не боля́ть но́ги.'?

'Боля́ть' is the form that always follows 'у'.
exercises.explanation: The body part is the subject of 'болі́ти', and the verb agrees with it. The person stands after 'у' in the genitive, so 'ме́не' cannot be the subject.

exercises.explanation: The 'я' form of 'му́сити' changes 'с' to 'ш': 'му́шу'. The other forms keep 'с': 'му́сиш', 'му́сить'.
'Пови́нен' is an adjective in its short form and agrees with the subject. Oksana is a woman, so the form is 'пови́нна'.
'Ва́рто' takes the person in the dative. Iryna Petrivna is addressed with 'ви', and the dative of 'ви' is 'вам'.

exercises.explanation: With 'ви', even to one woman, an adjective in the predicate is plural, so 'пови́нен' takes its plural form 'пови́нні'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Ти не му́сиш працюва́ти.' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Не му́сити' removes the obligation; it does not forbid. To forbid, Ukrainian uses 'не мо́жна' with the dative of the person.
